title: Poison hemlock
def: Poison hemlock is a deadly poisonous plant in the carrot family, often mistaken for wild carrot, parsley, or parsnip.
look: smooth, hairless, hollow stalk with purple blotches
fern-like, finely divided leaves that smell musty when crushed
clusters of small white flowers in umbrella shapes, up to 6 to 10 feet tall
use: Use this entry for identification and warnings only. Treat every wild carrot-family plant as dangerous unless an expert has confirmed it, and keep children and pets away.
not: Never eat, brew, or taste any part, and do not rely on boiling to make it safe.
alike: Wild carrot (Queen Anne's lace): hairy stem, carrot-smelling root, not blotched
Water hemlock: grows in wet ground, with chambered roots and veins running to leaf notches
Fool's parsley and wild parsnip: also unpleasant or harmful; do not guess
region: Poison hemlock is established across much of New England along roadsides, ditches, and field edges.
call: If someone may have eaten it, call 911 if they are very sick or Poison Control at 1-800-222-1222; do not wait for symptoms.

title: Wild carrot (Queen Anne's lace)
def: Wild carrot is a common white umbrella wildflower with hairy stems and a carrot-smelling root, and it is easy to confuse with deadly hemlocks.
look: hairy, solid stems
carrot smell from a crushed root or leaf
flat white flower head, sometimes with a single dark center floret, curling into a bird's nest when seeding
use: Use it only as an identification lesson. A beginner should not eat any carrot-family plant from the wild.
not: Do not eat it unless you can positively tell it from poison hemlock and water hemlock; a carrot smell alone is not enough when guessing.
alike: Poison hemlock: smooth, hairless, purple-blotched hollow stems; musty smell
Water hemlock: wet ground, chambered roots
Giant hogweed and wild parsnip: sap can cause severe skin burns in sunlight
call: If someone may have eaten a hemlock, call 911 if very sick, or Poison Control at 1-800-222-1222.

title: Water hemlock
also: deadly umbrella plant in wet ground
def: Water hemlock is one of the most poisonous plants in North America; a small amount of the root can cause fatal seizures.
look: grows in wet ground: stream banks, ditches, marshes
smooth hollow stems streaked or spotted with purple
doubly compound leaves with toothed leaflets whose veins run to the notches
a chambered root that oozes yellowish liquid when cut
use: Use only as a warning. Stay out of wet-ground carrot-family plants.
not: Never eat, taste, or handle the roots, and do not use it for a whistle or a straw.
alike: Wild carrot and poison hemlock: also in the carrot family
Wild parsnip and angelica: similar flowers and leaves
Edible-looking tubers or roots in wet ground: never eat them from the wild
call: Call 911 immediately for any ingestion; seizures can start within an hour.

title: Poison ivy
def: Poison ivy is a common plant of New England with three-leaflet leaves and an oil, urushiol, that causes an itchy, blistering rash on contact.
look: three leaflets, with the middle leaflet on a longer stalk
grows as a vine with hairy aerial roots, a shrub, or ground cover
leaves shiny or dull, edges smooth or notched, red in fall; white berries
use: Wash skin and clothing within minutes of contact and keep from touching your face. Learn it by sight, and look before you touch brush.
not: Never burn it; the smoke can injure the lungs. Do not pet a dog that has been in it without washing the coat.
alike: Virginia creeper: five leaflets
Box elder seedlings: leaflets in threes but opposite branching
Wild raspberry and blackberry: thorny stems
Poison sumac: swamp shrub with 7 to 13 leaflets
region: Poison ivy is abundant in New England woods, edges, and dunes; poison oak does not occur there.
call: Get care for a rash on the face or genitals, over much of the body, or with swelling or trouble breathing.

title: Poison sumac and poison oak
def: Poison sumac is a swamp shrub with 7 to 13 smooth-edged leaflets and white berries; it causes the same rash as poison ivy.
look: leaves of 7 to 13 smooth leaflets on a red stem
grows in wet swamps and bogs
drooping clusters of white-gray berries
use: Stay out of swamp shrubs you cannot name, and wash after contact like poison ivy.
not: Never burn it, and do not confuse it with harmless red-berried staghorn sumac.
alike: Staghorn sumac: upright red berry cones, toothed leaflets, dry ground
Poison ivy: three leaflets, vine or shrub
Poison oak: a western and southeastern plant, not in New England
call: Get care for a severe, facial, or widespread rash.

title: Never eat a wild mushroom from a photo
def: A photo, an app, or a camera match can never confirm a wild mushroom is safe; deadly species resemble edible ones, and cooking does not remove most toxins.
look: many deadly species look like edible ones
key features like spore print, base, and habitat do not show in a photo
apps and AI make mistakes
use: If you want to forage, learn from a local expert or a mycological society, and have every mushroom confirmed in person. If you are hungry and in trouble, use packed food and do not experiment.
not: Do not eat any wild mushroom from a photo, an app, a color rule, or a taste test, and do not give one to a child or pet.
call: Call Poison Control at 1-800-222-1222, or 911 if very sick, for any wild mushroom eaten by mistake; keep a sample.

title: Jack-o'-lantern mushroom (not a chanterelle)
def: The Jack-o'-lantern is an orange, poisonous mushroom that grows in clusters on wood and causes severe vomiting and cramps; it is often mistaken for a chanterelle.
look: orange, funnel-shaped caps growing in clusters from wood or buried roots
true, thin, sharp-edged gills running down the stem
grows on stumps or at the base of trees
use: Use as a warning example. If you find an orange mushroom, leave it, and do not eat anything you cannot confirm with an expert.
not: Do not eat any orange mushroom, and do not think a color or a glow in the dark confirms it.
alike: Chanterelle: single, from soil, blunt forked ridges (false gills), apricot smell, solid white flesh
Orange grocery produce and signs: not mushrooms; Yehsa does not identify them
Other orange mushrooms: do not guess
region: Jack-o'-lanterns are common in the eastern US in late summer and fall, on stumps and oak roots.
call: Call Poison Control at 1-800-222-1222 for any ingestion; call 911 if severely ill.

title: Chanterelle and its look-alikes
def: True chanterelles are golden, funnel-shaped mushrooms with blunt, forked ridges instead of thin gills, but only an expert should confirm them.
look: blunt, forked ridges that run down the stem and look like folds
grows from soil near trees, usually singly or scattered
fruity, apricot-like smell and solid white flesh inside
use: Learn them in person with a local expert or society, never from a photo.
not: Do not eat one that grows in dense clusters on wood, has thin sharp gills, or that you are not certain of.
alike: Jack-o'-lantern: clusters on wood, thin true gills
False chanterelle (Hygrophoropsis): thin, orange, forked true gills
Other orange mushrooms: do not guess
call: Call Poison Control at 1-800-222-1222 for any mistake; call 911 if very sick.

title: Destroying angel and death cap (deadly amanitas)
def: Destroying angels and death caps are deadly mushrooms; a small bite can destroy the liver, and symptoms may be delayed for hours.
look: white or greenish cap with white gills
a skirt-like ring on the stem and a cup or sac (volva) at the base, which may be buried
white spore print
use: Use as a warning: do not eat white woodland mushrooms, and dig, never cut, if you are learning with an expert.
not: Do not eat any mushroom with white gills, a ring, and a swollen base. A white 'button' in the woods is not a grocery mushroom.
alike: Grocery button mushrooms: pink to brown gills, no cup at the base
Edible puffballs: solid white inside, no gills or stem outline
Other white Amanita: all may be poisonous
region: Amanita species and the introduced death cap occur in New England woodlands, often near oaks and pines.
call: Call 911 or Poison Control at 1-800-222-1222 at once; stomach pain may pass, but the liver may fail days later.

title: Someone may have eaten a poisonous plant or mushroom
def: If someone may have eaten a poisonous plant or mushroom, call Poison Control or 911 immediately, before symptoms appear.
look: any wild plant or mushroom swallowed by a child or pet
vomiting, belly pain, drooling, confusion, or seizures
delayed symptoms hours later with deadly mushrooms
use: Call 911 if the person is very sick, unresponsive, or having a seizure; otherwise call Poison Control at 1-800-222-1222. Keep a sample or a photo and note the time and amount. Rinse the mouth and keep the person calm.
not: Do not make the person vomit, and do not wait for symptoms or a plant-ID app.
call: Call 911 or Poison Control at 1-800-222-1222 right away; for pets call a veterinarian or a pet poison line.

title: Is this plant safe to eat?
def: A wild plant is only safe to eat when a person has positively identified it by several features and ruled out its poisonous look-alikes; if you are unsure, the answer is no.
look: more than one feature checked: leaf, flower, fruit, stem, habitat
look-alikes ruled out
legal to harvest where you are
use: Use food you carried first. If you want to learn foraging, go with a local expert, use a regional guide, and start with the few plants that have no deadly look-alikes.
not: Do not eat unknown plants, do not use a camera or app as a yes, and do not use a taste test.
call: Call Poison Control at 1-800-222-1222 for any mistaken ingestion.

title: False rules about wild food
also: animals eat it so it is safe
def: Rules of thumb such as 'animals eat it', 'boiling makes it safe', or 'avoid red plants' are false and have killed people.
look: animals can eat plants that poison people
boiling does not destroy many toxins
berry color is not a safety rule
use: Do not use a universal edibility test for unknown plants. In a real emergency, focus on water, shelter, and signaling; people can go weeks without food.
not: Do not rely on color, taste, smell, animal behavior, or cooking.
call: Call Poison Control at 1-800-222-1222 for any mistake.

title: Toxic berries and fruits in New England
def: Several New England berries are poisonous, including baneberry, pokeweed, bittersweet nightshade, yew, and Virginia creeper.
look: baneberry: white or red berries with a dark dot on stalks
pokeweed: dark purple berries on pink stems
bittersweet nightshade: red egg-shaped berries on a vine
yew: red cup-shaped fruit with a toxic seed
use: Teach children not to eat any wild berry, and keep these plants out of reach. Leave unknown berries alone.
not: Do not eat unknown berries or pokeweed, and do not use berry color as a rule.
alike: Blueberries and blackberries: well-known edibles with a crown on blueberries
Wild raspberries: hollow when picked, thorny canes
Do not guess; confirm in person
call: Call Poison Control at 1-800-222-1222 for any berry eaten by mistake.

title: Blueberries, blackberries, and raspberries
def: Wild blueberries, blackberries, and raspberries are common New England fruits with few dangerous look-alikes, but always confirm them in person.
look: blueberry: small blue berry with a five-pointed crown on the end
blackberry and raspberry: clusters of tiny drupelets on thorny canes; raspberries pull off hollow
grows in sunny clearings, edges, and bogs
use: Pick only fruits you recognized in person, wash them, and pick where it is legal and where there is no spray.
not: Do not eat berries that do not match all features, and do not pick on private land without permission.
alike: Bittersweet nightshade: red egg-shaped berries on a vine
Pokeweed: purple berries on pink stems
Baneberry: white or red berries with dots
region: Wild lowbush blueberry barrens are a Maine specialty; check the land rules before you pick.
call: Call Poison Control at 1-800-222-1222 for mistaken ingestion.

title: True morel versus false morel
def: True morels have a honeycomb cap attached to a hollow stem, while false morels have a wrinkled, brain-like cap and cottony or chambered inside and can be toxic.
look: true morel: pitted honeycomb cap, hollow from tip to base when cut lengthwise
false morel: wrinkled, lobed cap that hangs free, with cottony or chambered interior
grows in spring under trees
use: Have an expert show you in person, and cut every specimen in half lengthwise. Cook any morel thoroughly; never eat raw.
not: Do not eat a morel-like mushroom whose inside is not fully hollow, and do not eat it raw.
alike: False morel (Gyromitra): toxic, cap hangs free
Half-free morel: edible but easy to confuse
call: Call Poison Control at 1-800-222-1222 after a mistaken ingestion.

title: Fiddleheads (ostrich fern)
def: Fiddleheads are the coiled young fronds of the ostrich fern, a spring food in Maine; they must be identified correctly and cooked thoroughly or they can cause illness.
look: a smooth stem with a deep U-shaped groove on the inside
brown papery scales on the coil
grows in clumps of about three from a single crown, near rivers
use: Learn them in person, pick small amounts, rinse off the brown scales, and cook thoroughly per public-health guidance (boil about 15 minutes or steam 10 to 12). If you are unsure, skip them.
not: Do not eat them raw or undercooked, and do not eat other fern species.
alike: Bracken fern: hairy stem with no deep groove, not recommended
Cinnamon fern: woolly coil with hairs
Other ferns: do not eat
region: Maine and the Northeast have a spring fiddlehead season along rivers; check state rules on harvest on public land.
call: Get care for vomiting or diarrhea after eating fiddleheads.

title: Acorns need proper leaching
def: Acorns are high in tannins that taste bitter and upset the stomach, so they must be shelled, ground, and leached in many changes of water before use.
look: bitter, astringent taste when raw
white oak acorns have less tannin
process with a sourced method only
use: If you want to use acorns, follow a sourced method and expect hours of leaching. In a survival situation, they are not a first food.
not: Do not eat acorns raw or with a short soak.

title: Wild nuts: hazelnut, beechnut, walnut, butternut
def: Hazelnuts, beechnuts, hickory nuts, black walnuts, and butternuts are native New England nuts, but they need positive identification and proper processing.
look: each tree has distinct leaves, bark, and husk
black walnut and butternut have thick, stain-prone husks
many nuts need drying and shelling
use: Identify the tree in person, check for allergies, shell and eat only sound nuts.
not: Do not eat moldy or discolored nuts, and do not eat a nut unless you know the tree.
region: Butternut is threatened by canker and is protected in some places; check local rules.

title: Cattail and its look-alikes
def: Cattails are tall wetland plants with brown sausage-shaped spikes, but young shoots can be confused with poisonous wild iris.
look: brown cylindrical flower spike above long flat leaves
grows in standing water or marshes
young shoots smell like cucumber, not musty
use: Learn them with an expert; cattails absorb pollutants, so use only from clean water.
not: Do not eat anything from polluted water, and do not eat a plant you cannot tell from iris.
alike: Wild iris (blue flag): flat, blue-green fans, no spike, toxic
Other marsh plants: do not guess
call: Call Poison Control at 1-800-222-1222 for a mistaken ingestion.

title: Dandelion and plantain greens
def: Dandelion and broadleaf plantain are common lawn and field weeds that can be eaten as greens when picked from clean, unsprayed places.
look: dandelion: toothed rosette leaves and a single hollow stem with one yellow flower
plantain: oval ribbed leaves in a rosette with a spike of seeds
picked far from roads, pets, and chemicals
use: Pick young leaves from clean, unsprayed ground, wash them, and cook or eat as a small addition, not as free calories.
not: Do not pick from roadsides, treated lawns, or dog areas.
alike: Cat's ear and hawkweed: look similar and are less well studied
Other rosette plants: confirm in person

title: Plants that poison by contact, eating, or smoke
def: Plants can harm by contact (poison ivy, wild parsnip, giant hogweed), by eating (hemlocks, baneberry), or by smoke (burning poison ivy).
look: wild parsnip and giant hogweed sap causes burns in sunlight
poison ivy oil causes a rash
hemlocks and baneberry are poisonous when eaten
use: Learn the plants of your area, wear long sleeves and gloves in brush, and wash exposed skin after contact. Keep children and pets from unknown plants.
not: Do not burn unknown brush, and do not touch sap from large umbrella plants without gloves.
region: Giant hogweed and wild parsnip occur in New England; avoid contact with their sap and sunlight.
call: Call 911 for trouble breathing or severe reactions; call Poison Control at 1-800-222-1222.
